newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cotton rates seen up in Pakistan, weak in India.
newsitem.headline: Cotton rates seen up in Pakistan, weak in India.

text.p: Cotton rates are likely to firm in Pakistan in the next week on foreign buying but ease in India on hopes of a higher crop, dealers said on Friday.

In Pakistan, the private Karachi Cotton Association (KCA) on Friday fixed the rate of good-quality NIAB-78 saw-ginned cotton from the new 1997/98 (July-June) crop at 2,543.13 rupees per maund (37.32 kg) on fresh buying by Brazil, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Portugal, Japan, Vietnam and Hong Kong, dealer Nasim Usman said.
The new rate for new crop was 196.88 rupees higher compared to Thursday's KCA close at 2,346.25 for the 1996/97 crop.
"The 1997/98 crop is good, therefore prices have gone up," he said.

Some 19,755 (375-lb) bales of cotton were registered for export in 10 days to July 28, raising export contracts to 190,080, the KCA said. The contracts were signed between $0.65 and $0.73 per lb FOB and $0.71 C&F for various destinations.
The KCA started the new-crop quotation and deleted the price of 1996/97 crop NIAB-78 from Friday, Usman said.
Spinners picked up buying from the new crop as they planned to build up stocks, Usman said.
New crop arrivals have risen and farmers say recent rains benefited the crop in the main-growing Punjab province, according to Usman.

Pakistan set a production target of 10 million bales for the 1997/98 crop, up from 8.783 million produced in 1996/97, when output fell from the 10 million bale target owing to untimely rains and pests.

In the kerb market, new-crop NIAB-78 was quoted from 2,540 to 2,550 rupees per maund.
In India, cotton prices remained weak in the week to Thursday, dealers said.

They said short- and medium-staple varieties suffered a setback but long-staple cotton remained exceptionally firm during the week. Prices initially firmed on reports of dry weather in cotton-producing centres after a break in monsoon rains.
"But a revival of the monsoon brought prices down," said Manubhai Amarsey, a leading cotton dealer.
India's cotton crop depends mostly on rains during the four-month June-September monsoon season.
Spot Bengal-deshi lost 5.0 rupees to 1,005/1,075 per maund (37.32 kg) and Punjab saw-ginned shed 5.0 to 1,820/1,855.
Gujarat Kalyan fell 400 rupees to 14,100/14,700 per candy (355.56 kg), Wagad dropped 100 to 13,000/13,100 and Kala-ginned shed 100 to 12,300/12,400 per candy.
Dealers said mills were holding stocks that could last for two to three months and this reduced their buying during the week.
"Expectations of a higher new crop for the 1997/1998 season (October/September) also subdued sentiment," Amarsey said.
India's 1996/97 cotton crop has been estimated at 16.78 million bales (170-kg), up from the previous year's 16.27 million. "It's too early to predict the size of the 1997/98 crop," Amarsey said.

Long-staple cotton remained firm in the week on a shortage of ready stock. Gujarat Sankar-4 long-staple (average variety) rose 400/500 rupees to 19,000/20,000 per candy and the superior variety made a similar gain to 20,500/21,500.
($1 = 40.62 Pakistani rupees)
